source.title: Switching: understanding the class-reversed sampling in tail sample memorization
source.authors: Chi Zhang; Benyi Hu; Yuhang Liuzhang; Le Wang; Li Liu; Yue-Hu Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how changing the training sampler affects test accuracy and reports sample-regularity measurements. These are related to the broad memorization/generalization topic, but they do not test any of V1–V8 as stated.
record.gate_note: The paper reports long-tailed classification accuracy, sampler comparisons, and regularity measurements. These bear on the broader claim topic but do not measure the behaviors specified in V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study measures sampler changes, long-tailed classification accuracy, and learning-event irregularity. None tests V1–V8: tail-sample oversampling is not removal based on label-memorization influence, and irregularity is not magnitude-aware sharpness. V1 and V8 appear as background citations.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors argue that switching from IB to CR at a small learning rate improves tail recognition while limiting head-class damage, and derive a conditional generalization-error upper-bound comparison. The bound is not an unconditional guarantee of lower realized test error.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes sampling during training on naturally long-tailed image datasets; it does not reproduce the interventions or measurements in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies with the dataset, imbalance ratio, and switching setting S. The authors state that class-reversed sampling alone can fail on some severely imbalanced settings, and that switching order matters.

fits_no_version.finding: Corrected Table 1 comparisons show Switching exceeds reproduced instance-balanced accuracy in all six CIFAR settings: 79.7 versus 73.1, 82.9 versus 77.9, 88.4 versus 86.4, 44.7 versus 40.7, 49.5 versus 44.9, and 59.5 versus 57.2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late IB-to-CR switching improves long-tailed CIFAR classification accuracy over the study's reproduced instance-balanced baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: At imbalance ratio 50, the reported S settings yield CIFAR-10 accuracies of 82.0–82.9 versus 77.9 and recorded CIFAR-100 accuracies of 47.5–49.5 versus 44.9. Large S settings require extended training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: IB-to-CR switching improves accuracy across the tested switching times, with gains varying by timing and training duration.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 12 reports Pearson correlation −0.6112 between class cardinality and the defined irregularity measure on long-tailed CIFAR-10, imbalance ratio 50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Class cardinality is negatively associated with normalized learning-event irregularity in this setting.

record.problems: No uncertainty intervals or statistical significance are reported for the tabulated accuracy results. The regularity relationship is measured in a specific long-tailed CIFAR-10 setting; it is not a direct measurement of a train-test error gap. Some comparator results in the main performance table are copied from other papers, as indicated in its notes.
record.rows_left_out: Additional sampler-combination results in Tables 6–8, fine-grained class-group accuracy in Table 4, and test-accuracy and bias/variance comparisons in Tables 2–3 and 9–11 are not included. The 60-row limit was not reached; these results were left out because the selected rows cover the principal switching effect, its S variation, and the reported class-irregularity measurements.

untested.parts: Matched random-label and natural-label training, training fit, and held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and competing measures.
Influence-based identification and removal of memorized examples versus random removal, followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tests/T2 classification conflicts with its correct observation that no version is tested. R1–R6 misread the reproduced cross-entropy row as Switching, creating a spurious reversal. All states here concern applicability to V1–V8. The paper calls the negative correlation one with regularity, but its formula and Table 12 measure irregularity; no significance test is supplied.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy under the same recipes.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Large versus small batch training and adaptations to the recipe.
Effects of dropout and its removal.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
